title: Machine Learning in Epidemiology with R — Part 2
text:
What will we learn?
Can clinical measurements help us distinguish patients with and without heart disease? We will first read the results of a random forest already fitted to these data. Then we will build a neural network and examine its predictions.
By the end, you should be able to explain a model’s mistakes, fit a neural network with Keras, and use mlr3 to evaluate its predictions.
Have the session guide ready before starting. It covers opening the project and installing Keras. The code below assumes your working folder is part2/. Run the code blocks in order in RStudio during the session. Saved results let us discuss the examples before fitting our own network.

title: Machine Learning in Epidemiology with R — Part 2
text:
1. Meet the heart data
Each row describes one patient. There are 270 patients and 13 measurements, including age, chest pain and cholesterol. The outcome, heart_disease, tells us whether heart disease is absent or present. We are classifying existing heart disease, rather than estimating future risk.
Load the prepared data. The data script gives the categories readable labels.

# Load the patient measurements and outcome labels.
source("R/01-data.R")

Count the patients in each outcome group:

table(heart$heart_disease)


 absent present 
    150     120 


There are 150 patients without heart disease and 120 with heart disease. A predictor is a measurement we use to help predict the outcome. The outcome itself must not be included among the predictors.
Discuss: Which measurements might help distinguish the two groups?






NoteDiscussion: possible predictors





Chest-pain type, exercise-induced angina, maximum heart rate and exercise ECG measurements are plausible candidates. The vessel count and thal test result may also help distinguish the groups. Age, blood pressure and cholesterol may contribute alongside these measurements. These are starting hypotheses, not a computed ranking of importance. We need data and evaluation to establish which patterns help prediction in this sample. Predictive usefulness does not establish that a measurement causes disease.



For a visual explanation of single trees, see the optional Trees and pruning companion. It explains Figures 1–3 and why pruning can leave a tree looking similar to the default tree.

title: Machine Learning in Epidemiology with R — Part 2
text:
2. Read the random forest results
A random forest combines predictions from many decision trees. We have already fitted this model using 180 patients and tested it on the other 90. The test patients were kept out of training so we could assess predictions on unseen observations. We will use the saved results here, without fitting the forest again.

What did the model get right and wrong?
A confusion matrix counts correct predictions and mistakes. Read the rows as the model’s predictions and the columns as the patients’ recorded outcomes.


Read the saved confusion matrix
forest_confusion <- read.csv("outputs/confusion.csv")
forest_table <- xtabs(Freq ~ response + truth, data = forest_confusion)
knitr::kable(forest_table, caption = "Random forest: predictions for 90 test patients")



Random forest: predictions for 90 test patients



absent
present




absent
45
7


present
8
30





The model correctly identified 30 patients with heart disease and 45 without it. It missed 7 patients who had heart disease (false negatives) and raised 8 false alarms in patients without heart disease (false positives).
Discuss: What might a missed case mean for a patient? What might a false alarm lead to?


How well did it perform?
Accuracy is the proportion of all test patients classified correctly. Sensitivity is the proportion of patients with heart disease correctly identified. Specificity is the proportion without heart disease correctly identified.


Read the saved forest scores
forest_scores <- read.csv("outputs/holdout-measures.csv")
measure_ids <- c("classif.acc", "classif.tpr", "classif.tnr")
measure_labels <- c("Accuracy", "Sensitivity", "Specificity")
forest_values <- forest_scores$value[match(measure_ids, forest_scores$measure)]

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(Measure = measure_labels, Percent = round(100 * forest_values, 1)),
  caption = "Saved random forest results (%)"
)



Saved random forest results (%)


Measure
Percent




Accuracy
83.3


Sensitivity
81.1


Specificity
84.9





Accuracy is 83.3%: 75 correct predictions out of 90. Sensitivity is 81.1% and specificity is 84.9%. Looking at all three helps us see what accuracy alone can hide.
The forest predicts probabilities. A threshold is the probability at which we decide to classify a patient as having heart disease. Lowering the threshold usually catches more cases, but also raises more false alarms.



The ROC curve shows sensitivity against the false-positive rate as the probability threshold changes. The diagonal represents chance-level discrimination.


Discuss: Would you choose a threshold using accuracy alone?


How to read the evaluation curves
The ROC curve (Figure 4) compares sensitivity with the false-positive rate (1 − specificity) as the probability threshold changes. The saved curve sits above the diagonal: it shows useful discrimination on these test patients. The upper-left corner represents high sensitivity with few false alarms. The curve does not identify a clinically appropriate cut-off on its own.






NoteFigure 4 extensions: precision–recall and thresholds





The optional script also saves two other views of the same forest predictions. Recall is sensitivity, and precision is positive predictive value: the share of positive predictions that are correct. Their curve shows the balance as the threshold changes; precision also depends on disease frequency.
The threshold plot shows classification error, the fraction of incorrect predictions, for different cut-offs. A lower point means fewer total mistakes on these test patients. It does not give separate sensitivity/specificity curves or establish an optimal clinical threshold. Missed cases and false alarms can have different consequences. Choose a threshold using training/validation data and a stated purpose, then assess it on separate evaluation data.



Saved forest precision–recall curve for the 90 test patients.





Saved forest classification error across probability thresholds.







Why move to a neural network?
The forest provides a baseline. A neural network gives us a different way to learn from the same measurements: trees divide patients into groups, whereas a network learns weighted combinations of inputs. We explore whether that change affects accuracy and the types of mistake. We keep the test patients consistent; adding complexity does not guarantee better predictions.

title: Machine Learning in Epidemiology with R — Part 2
section: 3. Use mlr3 to organise the prediction task
text:
3. Use mlr3 to organise the prediction task
We now ask the same question using a neural network. We keep the same training and test patients so the results can be compared.
mlr3 helps organise a prediction problem. A task records the data and the outcome we want to predict. Here, present is the positive class: the condition we want to detect. We load the saved split instead of drawing a new one.

library(mlr3)
# Tell mlr3 which outcome to predict and which class means disease is present.
heart_task <- as_task_classif(heart,
  target = "heart_disease",
  positive = "present",
  id = "heart"
)
# Reuse the patients used to train and test the saved random forest.
split_record <- read.csv("outputs/split.csv")
split <- list(
  train = split_record$row_id[split_record$subset == "train"],
  test = split_record$row_id[split_record$subset == "test"]
)

The training group contains 180 patients; the test group contains 90. Keep the test patients aside until the network has finished learning.

Why separate a task from a learner?
A task defines the prediction problem: the dataset, outcome and positive class. A learner defines the method used to learn predictions. In script 2, lrn("classif.ranger", predict_type = "prob") creates a random-forest learner; train() fits it on the training rows and predict() evaluates other rows. The task itself does not create the split.
In script 3, we define the task again and reuse the saved row numbers, but Keras builds and trains the neural network directly. We do not create an mlr3 neural-network learner here. Later, PredictionClassif lets mlr3 evaluate Keras predictions with the same measures as the forest.
If you explored the tree plots first, the transition is from understanding fitted structure to evaluating predictions. The forest is a new model combining many trees; it does not reuse the single rpart tree we plotted.

title: Machine Learning in Epidemiology with R — Part 2
text:
4. Prepare the inputs
Keras needs numerical inputs. We turn categories into numbers and indicator columns. An indicator is a column containing 0 or 1 to show whether a category applies. This gives us 22 input columns from the original 13 predictors.
We also scale numerical measurements so differences in units, such as age and cholesterol, do not dominate the learning process. Scaling is learned from the fitting rows only, keeping validation and test patients out of that step.


Show input preparation
# Exclude the outcome from the inputs. Keras needs numbers, so use 0/1 for
# binary categories and indicator columns for the others. An indicator is 1
# when a category applies and 0 otherwise. Together these give 22 inputs.
x_data <- heart[, setdiff(names(heart), "heart_disease")]
for (nm in c("sex", "fasting_blood_sugar", "exercise_induced_angina")) {
  x_data[[nm]] <- as.integer(x_data[[nm]]) - 1L
}
nominal <- names(x_data)[vapply(x_data, is.factor, logical(1))]
contrasts_full <- lapply(x_data[nominal], function(x) contrasts(x, contrasts = FALSE))
x <- model.matrix(~ . - 1, data = x_data, contrasts.arg = contrasts_full)
stopifnot(ncol(x) == 22L, all(is.finite(x)))
# Keras reserves the last 20% of training rows for validation.
# Calculate scaling from the other 80% only, keeping validation and test
# patients out of this calculation.
inner_n <- floor(length(split$train) * 0.8)
fit_rows <- split$train[seq_len(inner_n)]
continuous <- names(x_data)[vapply(x_data, is.numeric, logical(1))]
continuous <- setdiff(
  continuous,
  c("sex", "fasting_blood_sugar", "exercise_induced_angina")
)
# Subtract each measurement's mean and divide by its standard deviation.
# This puts measurements with different units on a comparable scale.
centre <- colMeans(x[fit_rows, continuous, drop = FALSE])
spread <- apply(x[fit_rows, continuous, drop = FALSE], 2, sd)
stopifnot(all(spread > 0))
x[, continuous] <- sweep(
  sweep(x[, continuous, drop = FALSE], 2, centre),
  2, spread, "/"
)
# Code the outcome as 1 for present and 0 for absent.
y <- as.integer(heart$heart_disease == "present")


Check the number of input columns and the outcome coding:

ncol(x)
table(y)

The outcome is coded as 1 for heart disease and 0 for its absence.

Why are there 22 inputs?
model.matrix(~ . - 1, data = x_data, contrasts.arg = contrasts_full) creates one numerical row per patient. In the formula, . includes all predictors and - 1 removes the intercept column. contrasts_full requests an indicator for every level of each remaining categorical predictor.



Original predictors
Columns in x




Six numerical measurements/counts
6


Three binary predictors, already converted to 0/1
3


Chest-pain type (4), resting ECG (3), ST slope (3), thal (3)
13


Total
22



For example, a patient with typical angina has 1 in that chest-pain indicator column and 0 in the other three. The result is a 270 × 22 matrix. The outcome is excluded from x and stored separately in y.


What do centre, spread and sweep do?
centre stores each selected column’s mean among the 144 fitting patients. spread stores its standard deviation, a measure of variation. We standardise each continuous column using:
centred value = original value − fitting mean
scaled value = centred value / fitting standard deviation
The inner sweep() subtracts centre; subtraction is its default operation. The outer sweep() divides by spread using "/". The argument 2 means operate column by column. drop = FALSE keeps the selection as a matrix even if only one column is selected. The assignment writes the scaled values back into the continuous columns of x, leaving binary and indicator columns unchanged.
For a conceptual example, a fitting mean age of 55 and standard deviation of 10 would transform age 65 into (65 − 55) / 10 = 1. These example values are illustrative, not summaries calculated from our data.
We apply the same fitting means and standard deviations to validation and test patients. This puts measurements with different units on comparable scales without using those patients to estimate the scaling. Once x and y are ready, we can define the network.

title: Machine Learning in Epidemiology with R — Part 2
text:
5. Build the network with Keras
Keras defines and trains the neural network. We use it directly here, then bring its predictions into mlr3 for evaluation.
Think of the network as a sequence:
Patient measurements → hidden layers → probability of heart disease
A hidden layer combines inputs into patterns that the network learns. The final layer returns one probability between 0 and 1. The two hidden layers below contain 64 and 32 units. Dropout temporarily switches off some units during training to help limit overfitting: learning the training examples too closely to work well on new patients.

library(keras3)
# Fix the random starting point for the network.
set_random_seed(20261023)

# Pass 22 inputs through two hidden layers to one output probability.
# Dropout temporarily switches off some units during training to limit overfitting.
network <- keras_model_sequential(input_shape = c(22)) |>
  layer_dense(units = 64, activation = "relu") |>
  layer_dropout(rate = 0.4) |>
  layer_dense(units = 32, activation = "relu") |>
  layer_dropout(rate = 0.4) |>
  layer_dense(units = 1, activation = "sigmoid")
# Choose how to update the weights and measure prediction error.
# Binary cross-entropy is a loss for a two-class outcome.
compile(network,
  optimizer = optimizer_adam(learning_rate = 0.002),
  loss = "binary_crossentropy", metrics = "accuracy"
)

compile() sets how the network learns. The optimiser updates its weights (the values controlling its connections). The loss measures prediction error; binary cross-entropy is used for this two-class outcome.

What does each layer do?
keras_model_sequential(input_shape = c(22)) defines a model whose layers connect in order. Each patient supplies 22 numbers; 22 is the number of input columns, not the number of patients. A container created with only this input shape can show no layers and zero parameters. The dense layers add the trainable weights.







Component
Role in this network




Dense, 64 units, ReLU
Each unit combines all 22 inputs using learned weights and a bias. ReLU keeps positive signals and returns zero for negative ones, allowing nonlinear patterns.


Dropout, rate 0.4
Randomly sets 40% of the preceding layer’s outputs to zero at each training step to help limit overfitting.


Dense, 32 units, ReLU
Learns further combinations of the signals from the preceding layer.


Dropout, rate 0.4
Also regularises the second hidden layer.


Dense, 1 unit, sigmoid
Converts the final signal into a value between 0 and 1, interpreted as an estimated probability of disease present.



Dense means every unit connects to every output of the preceding layer. Dropout operates during training and switches off for prediction. The 64/32 units and 0.4 dropout follow the reference architecture; they are settings we could investigate through tuning, rather than proven optimal choices. The complete architecture has 3,585 trainable parameters, including biases.
The architecture defines the calculation. compile() selects the learning rules: Adam updates the weights, and binary cross-entropy measures probability prediction error. fit() is the step that learns the weights from patients.






NoteIf creating the model takes time





The first Keras call in a fresh R session may also initialise Python and the backend. Creating the model container does not train the network. A persistent wait or an error warrants checking the Keras setup in the session guide; it is not evidence that 22 inputs are too many.

title: Machine Learning in Epidemiology with R — Part 2
section: 6. Fit the network and watch it learn
text:
6. Fit the network and watch it learn
An epoch is one pass through the fitting data. A batch is a smaller group processed before updating the weights.
We reserve 20% of the training group for validation: checking progress during learning. The network updates its weights using 144 patients and monitors its progress on 36 validation patients. These are separate from the 90 test patients. Early stopping ends training if validation loss stops improving.

# An epoch is one pass through the fitting rows; batches contain 32 rows.
# Monitor validation loss and stop after 10 epochs without improvement,
# restoring the weights from the best validation epoch.
training <- fit(
  network,
  x[split$train, ],
  y[split$train],
  epochs = 50,
  batch_size = 32,
  validation_split = 0.2,
  verbose = 1,
  callbacks = list(callback_early_stopping(patience = 10, restore_best_weights = TRUE))
)

Plot the history from your own run:

# Compare training and validation loss as learning progresses.
plot(training)

Look for training and validation loss in this plot. The figure below comes from the saved workshop run; your run may produce a different curve.



Saved neural-network run: training and validation loss across successive passes through the fitting data. Lower loss means smaller prediction error.


If training loss keeps falling while validation loss rises, the network may be overfitting.
Discuss: Why do we need validation patients as well as training patients?

Why keep fitting, validation and test patients separate?








Group
Patients
What we use them for




Fitting
144
Update the network weights using prediction errors.


Validation
36
Monitor learning and select the stopping epoch, without updating weights from these rows.


Test
90
Assess predictions after fitting and model choices are complete.



Training error alone can fall because the network learns details of its examples. Validation asks whether those improvements also help patients outside the weight updates. Because validation influences the stopping decision, it cannot replace the final test group. Early stopping uses patience 10: after ten epochs without improvement in validation loss, training ends and restores the best weights.


How to read Figure 5
The blue curve is fitting/training loss and the red curve is validation loss. Both initially fall, suggesting that learning also helps the validation patients. Later, training loss continues downward, while validation loss levels off and rises slightly. More training is then improving the fit without improving validation performance, a warning of overfitting.
The saved history contains 27 epochs; its lowest validation loss occurs at epoch 17. This agrees with stopping after ten further epochs without improvement. These are the saved run’s curves, not a guarantee for a new run.
This connects to tree pruning: both pruning and early stopping help control complexity, through different mechanisms. Neither proves performance on new patients; the separate test group supplies the final evaluation.

title: Machine Learning in Epidemiology with R — Part 2
section: 7. Evaluate the network and compare results
text:
7. Evaluate the network and compare results
Use the trained network to predict probabilities for the 90 test patients. For this example, classify a probability of 0.5 or more as present.
PredictionClassif$new() puts the Keras predictions into an mlr3 prediction object. It stores the observed outcomes, predicted classes and probabilities. We can then request the same measures used for the forest.

# Predict unseen test patients. Use 0.5 as the cut-off for a present prediction.
prob <- as.numeric(predict(network, x[split$test, ], verbose = 0))
class <- ifelse(prob >= 0.5, "present", "absent")
accuracy <- mean(class == as.character(heart$heart_disease[split$test]))
accuracy

# Bring the Keras predictions into mlr3 for the same evaluation measures.
network_pred <- PredictionClassif$new(
  task = heart_task,
  row_ids = split$test,
  truth = heart_task$truth(rows = split$test),
  response = class,
  prob = cbind(present = prob, absent = 1 - prob)
)
network_pred$confusion
network_pred$score(msrs(c("classif.acc", "classif.tpr", "classif.tnr")))


What happened in the saved run?
The next table uses the saved network predictions, rather than fitting a new network when the page opens.


Compare the saved results
saved_network <- read.csv("outputs/neural-predictions.csv")
stopifnot(
  identical(saved_network$row_id, split$test),
  identical(saved_network$truth, as.character(heart$heart_disease[split$test]))
)
saved_prediction <- PredictionClassif$new(
  task = heart_task,
  row_ids = saved_network$row_id,
  truth = heart_task$truth(rows = saved_network$row_id),
  response = saved_network$prediction,
  prob = cbind(
    present = saved_network$probability_present,
    absent = 1 - saved_network$probability_present
  )
)
network_values <- unname(saved_prediction$score(msrs(measure_ids)))
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Measure = measure_labels,
    `Random forest (%)` = round(100 * forest_values, 1),
    `Neural network (%)` = round(100 * network_values, 1),
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  caption = "Saved results for the same 90 test patients"
)



Saved results for the same 90 test patients


Measure
Random forest (%)
Neural network (%)




Accuracy
83.3
85.6


Sensitivity
81.1
78.4


Specificity
84.9
90.6





The saved network classified 77 of the 90 test patients correctly, compared with 75 for the forest. That small difference in one split does not establish that neural networks are generally better. Compare the types of mistakes as well as the overall accuracy. After your own run, use network_pred above to inspect your results; this saved comparison table remains a reference.
Discuss: Which model missed fewer cases? Is the difference large enough to change your conclusion?


What improved, and what did not?



Saved test result
Random forest
Keras network




Correct predictions
75/90
77/90


Missed disease cases
7
8


False alarms
8
5



Network accuracy increased by 2.2 percentage points after rounding. It made three fewer false alarms but missed one more disease case. Whether that balance is preferable depends on the purpose and consequences of the prediction.
We evaluated the random forest and Keras network here. The single-tree plots illustrate fitting and pruning; they do not provide a third held-out score. Both evaluated models use the same 90 test patients, but the forest fits on all 180 training patients and the network uses 144 for fitting plus 36 for validation. The models also use different input representations. These saved local runs support a teaching comparison, not a controlled demonstration that one method is generally superior.
A prediction estimates the recorded outcome from measurements. It does not identify what caused the patient’s disease, and this example does not forecast future cardiovascular risk.

title: Machine Learning in Epidemiology with R — Part 2
text:
Where to go next
The main session ends here. Choose an extension when you want to explore a specific question further:



Question
Follow-up material




How does a single tree work, and why simplify it?
Trees and pruning companion, with the R script


Would another training sample give different results?
Resampling in the same script


Can different model settings improve predictions?
Tuning


Which measurements influence predictions?
Discuss feature importance and effects; predictive importance does not establish causation.


Can we create artificial records resembling these patients?
Synthetic data: generate the records, then compare age summaries and outcome proportions with heart.



These scripts run separately. The tree/evaluation script also refits the random forest; it is not needed for the main session.

Resampling: how stable are the results?
Cross-validation rotates which group stays out of fitting. Repeated subsampling uses different splits; bootstrap samples fitting rows with replacement. Script 2 includes three-fold cross-validation, 100 subsampling repetitions and 40 bootstrap repetitions for a 100-tree forest, evaluating AUC. Those scores use a different measure and evaluation design from the main holdout accuracy comparison.
For a new model comparison, use the same folds and measures for both methods. Estimate preprocessing inside each fitting fold and keep model/threshold selection separate from evaluation. Repeatedly changing a model to improve the test results we have already examined would weaken that test set’s independence.


Tuning: can different settings help?
Script 4 tunes an XGBoost model, a boosted-tree method; it does not tune the Keras network or the main random forest. It searches over the number and depth of trees, learning rate and regularisation strength. Grid search tries a fixed collection of settings, random search samples settings, and model-based optimisation uses earlier trials to guide the next ones. Ten-fold cross-validation within the training group compares candidate settings.
Nested cross-validation separates selection from evaluation: inner folds choose settings and outer folds assess the whole selection process. The saved validation record reports completed 500-configuration random search and 30-configuration model-based search. The full grid and full-budget nested workflow have only had reduced smoke tests; they are not completed full runs. Tuning does not guarantee an improvement. See the validation record before running these potentially long extensions.


Synthetic data: what do artificial records represent?
Script 5 uses an adversarial random forest to learn patterns in the observed data. forde() estimates a distribution from the fitted forest, and forge() samples 270 artificial records from it. The generated table is saved separately as outputs/synthetic-heart.csv.
Compare age summaries and outcome proportions with the real data as an initial check, then consider relationships between variables and the intended use. Synthetic records are examples for exploration and teaching, not additional observed patients or independent evidence of predictive performance. Generating them does not automatically guarantee privacy.

title: Part 2 — Heart-disease data
text:
Source: OpenML heart-statlog, ID 53, version 1. Downloaded 12 October 2026 from the URL in the saved OpenML metadata. The metadata lists the licence as Public. The original data are attributed to Janosi, Steinbrunn, Pfisterer and Detrano (1988), as cited by the article.
The snapshot has 270 patients, 13 predictors and a binary target: 150 absent, 120 present. It is the OpenML Statlog heart dataset matching the article’s sample size, predictor definitions and outcome.
raw/heart-statlog.arff is unchanged. SHA-256: e16082cc6158f29be2e7b081953cd6edf342760d135bccdb64e191d0834d6300. raw/openml-53-metadata.json preserves the source metadata. processed/heart.csv is regenerated by R/01-data.R.
ARFF (Attribute–Relation File Format) is a text format with a section describing column names and types, followed by the data, with one patient per row. The raw file is the original download before workshop preparation. The preparation script reads it, assigns readable column names and categories, and saves the prepared data as processed/heart.csv.

title: Part 2 — Heart-disease data
text:
Preprocessing
The ARFF target already uses absent/present. The preparation script renames predictors to the article’s appendix names and applies its category definitions. No rows are removed and no imputation is needed. The seven categorical fields are sex, chest_pain, fasting_blood_sugar, resting_ecg, exercise_induced_angina, ST_slope and thal. The other six are explicitly numeric, including the vessel count, as in the appendix.
For the neural network, the three binary predictors use 0/1 and the four other categorical predictors use full indicator encoding, giving 22 columns. Full indicator encoding of all seven categorical predictors would give 25 columns. The article states 22 inputs but does not publish the encoding implementation. Our 22-column construction is therefore an explicit reconstruction. Numeric scaling is fitted on the inner training portion, excluding validation and test rows; scaling details are not specified in the published example. For XGBoost, fixed categorical contrasts produce a numeric design matrix.
The outcome describes heart disease in this teaching sample. It is not a population cardiovascular risk score or a future-event endpoint.

title: Part 2 — Source and replication record
text:
Workshop implementation
The scripts define data preparation, train/test objects and tuning code, use heart_task consistently and set explicit seeds. Keras uses keras3 instead of the article’s older keras interface, retaining the architecture and training settings. The network now reads outputs/split.csv to reuse the forest’s saved training/test patients explicitly. Keras predictions are wrapped in an mlr3 PredictionClassif object to evaluate both models using the same measures. Data encoding/scaling choices are recorded in the data guide. Random-forest threading is fixed to one for reproducibility. The initial forest uses the learner default; the resampling examples use 100 trees, as printed. Tuning is restricted to the training task; nested CV uses an outer and inner 10-fold design. The article’s full grid has up to 10,000 configurations and is not run during a normal notebook render.
The article reports a 100% neural-network test accuracy. That is a reported result for its run, not an expected or guaranteed workshop result. Our outputs are saved separately. Results depend on the random seed, data split, preprocessing and software versions.

title: How a Model Learns in Epidemiology
text:
Slide presentation
Open the Part 1 presentation Download the PDF
The slide deck introduces the broader multi-model workflow. The model-performance and variable-importance values shown in the deck are illustrative. The executable notebook below contains the observed results.
By the end, we should be able to answer four questions:

What is the model?
What is the loss?
What is the optimisation procedure?
What is learned?

The central message is:

Learning means using data to determine a model’s parameters or structure. Optimisation is the procedure used to find useful values or structures according to an objective.

title: Machine Learning in Epidemiology with R — Part 2
section: What have we learned about machine learning?
text:
What have we learned about machine learning?
Machine learning uses examples to learn a rule for making predictions. We choose the outcome, available inputs, model structure and learning procedure; the algorithm uses fitting data to determine its internal rules or values. A tree learns splits, a forest combines many trees, and a neural network learns connection weights.
The full workflow is to prepare inputs, fit the model, monitor validation and assess predictions on patients outside fitting. A lower training error alone is insufficient. We consider accuracy alongside the kinds of mistake, and keep our conclusions within the limits of one small dataset and one test split.
The main session can end here. Resampling would next ask how stable the results are when the patients used for fitting and evaluation change.

title: Part 2 — Trees and pruning
text:
Return to the Part 2 teaching notebook
This optional companion explains the figures produced by R/02-trees-and-evaluation.R. The main session reads saved forest results and then builds a neural network. You do not need to run this extension script during that lesson: it also refits the forest and runs resampling, replacing its saved outputs.

title: Part 2 — Trees and pruning
section: Figure 1: how the default tree divides patients
text:
Figure 1: how the default tree divides patients



Figure 1. Default classification tree fitted to all 270 patients.


Read the tree from top to bottom. Each split asks a question about a measurement. Follow the branch that matches the patient’s value until reaching a terminal node, or leaf, which supplies the prediction.
The first split uses the thal test result. A normal result follows the left branch; the other results follow the right branch. Later splits use chest-pain type, number of major vessels, exercise-induced angina and age.
Each node shows the predicted class (absent or present), the proportion with disease among patients reaching that node, and the percentage of all patients reaching it. At the top, 0.44 means about 44% of the 270 patients have disease. The predicted class there is absent, the majority group. Blue leaves predict absence and green leaves predict presence; the displayed proportions indicate that the groups are not necessarily pure.
Checkpoint: Follow one path from the top to a leaf. Which combination of measurements determines its prediction?
The tree uses all 270 patients to illustrate fitted structure. The apparent separation in its leaves is not a held-out estimate of performance on new patients.

title: Part 2 — Trees and pruning
text:
Figure 2: complexity and cross-validation error



Figure 2. Relative cross-validation error as the larger tree becomes more complex.


The bottom axis shows the complexity parameter, cp. Moving right permits smaller values of cp and more splits. The top axis shows the number of terminal leaves. The vertical axis shows relative cross-validation error: lower values indicate smaller estimated error. It is a relative error, not an accuracy percentage. The vertical bars show one standard error on either side of each estimate.
Error falls sharply after the first few splits and then changes relatively little as the tree gains branches. This suggests that a simpler tree may retain much of the useful structure.
The dotted line marks one standard error above the lowest estimated error. A common rule chooses the smallest tree whose error falls below that line, accepting similar estimated performance with less complexity. In this workshop, cp = 0.031 retains the article’s setting; we should distinguish that replication choice from selecting a value using this plot.
Checkpoint: Would adding branches be persuasive if cross-validation error barely changes?

title: Part 2 — Trees and pruning
text:
Figure 3: what pruning actually removed



Figure 3. Tree obtained by pruning the larger tree at cp = 0.031.


We did prune the tree. Figures 1 and 3 look similar because they retain the same main branches, but they represent different trees:



Tree
Splits
Leaves




Figure 1: default
6
7


Larger tree, before pruning
15
16


Figure 3: pruned
5
6



The default tree uses rpart() with its default controls. The larger tree uses rpart.control(minsplit = 2). We then call prune(deep_cart, cp = 0.031) to obtain Figure 3.
Pruning starts from the larger tree with 15 splits and 16 terminal nodes, not from the default tree in Figure 1. The displayed comparison therefore makes the reduction look smaller than it is.
Compared with Figure 1, the age >= 51 split on the right has disappeared. Those patients now share a single leaf. The main splits on thal, chest pain, vessel count and exercise-induced angina remain.
Pruning limits complexity by removing branches that may fit details of this sample. A simpler tree is easier to follow and may generalise better, but the act of pruning does not establish that it predicts new patients more accurately.






NoteCheck the tree sizes in R





Run this only after creating cart, deep_cart and pruned_cart in the tree section of script 2. It inspects the fitted objects without running the later forest/resampling sections.
models <- list(default = cart, larger = deep_cart, pruned = pruned_cart)
data.frame(
  tree = names(models),
  splits = vapply(models, function(m) sum(m$frame$var != "<leaf>"), integer(1)),
  leaves = vapply(models, function(m) sum(m$frame$var == "<leaf>"), integer(1))
)

title: Part 2 — Trees and pruning
section: From tree plots to mlr3 evaluation
text:
From tree plots to mlr3 evaluation
The plots ask how a fitted model makes decisions. The next question is how well a model predicts patients it did not learn from.
In script 2, mlr3 defines a classification task with heart_disease as the outcome and present as the positive class. A learner specifies the method: classif.ranger is a random forest that combines many trees. It does not reuse the single plotted tree.
The saved split assigns 180 patients to training and 90 to testing. Fitting the forest on the training rows and predicting the test rows gives a held-out assessment. The saved forest correctly classified 75 of 90 test patients, missed 7 disease cases and raised 8 false alarms. These are forest results, not test scores for the default or pruned single trees.
The main notebook then introduces Keras as another learning method and evaluates its predictions on the same 90 test patients. Pruning and the network’s early stopping are different ways to control complexity. Resampling is a further step for examining how stable results are across samples.
Continue with the saved forest results

No forest, Keras model or tuning search was rerun for this explanation, and saved workshop outputs were preserved.
